newsitem.title: USA: Restored Grant's tomb unveiled in New York.
newsitem.headline: Restored Grant's tomb unveiled in New York.

text.p: Exactly a century after one million spectators witnessed the dedication of the granite monument to Ulysses S. Grant, thousands gathered on Sunday to celebrate the completion of its renovation.

Ulysses Grant Dietz, great-great-grandson of the Civil War hero, was among those taking part in a two-day centennial celebration commemorating the renovation of the towering monument where the body of the 18th U.S. President rests, in an imposing tomb on the upper West Side of Manhattan just east of the Hudson River.

"The National Park Service has spent upwards of $1.8 million on construction, new ceilings, new roofs, waterproofing the building, painting, masonry as well as a new plaza," Manny Strumpf, a spokesman for the Park Service said.

The granite structure erected in Grant's memory on April 27, 1897 became a National Monument in 1959. At one time the monument drew about 100,000 visitors annually to the rotunda and to view its 150-foot dome and three murals including Robert E. Lee's surrender to Grant at Appomattox.
But as government money and interest in the tomb slipped, the structure became a haven for the homeless, graffiti artists and vandals.
By the early 1990s, a crisis developed when a Park Service volunteer who worked at the monument blew the whistle and alerted the media to its deteriorating condition.

The volunteer, Frank Scaturro, was fired for exposing the mess and it was not until Grant's descendants threatened to remove the bodies of Grant and his wife Julia and rebury them in the Midwest that the government launched the renovation project.

For his role in spearheading the drive to compel the government to restore Grant's Tomb, Scaturro and the Grant Monument Association, a private group he formed, was banned from taking part in Sunday's celebration.
According to Scaturro, who was barred by the Park Service from placing a wreath in tribute to Grant, the snub was in retaliation for his going public over the tomb's condition.

To celebrate the 100th anniversary of the tomb and the 175th anniversary of Grant's birth on April 27, 1822 in Point Pleasant, Ohio, hundreds of bands were brought in to play, including the marching band from the U.S. Military Academy, cadets firing a 21-gun salute and Grant's high school bands from Portland, Oregon and Portsmouth, Ohio.
Grant, a Republican who served two terms as president, had been regarded as a failure until he became a soldier.

He ultimately captured the nation's attention when a Confederate commander asked for the terms upon which to surrender Fort Donelson in Tennessee. Grant replied: "An unconditional and immediate surrender." After that, he became "U.S. Grant - Unconditional Surrender Grant."
Grant, the nation's most beloved General since George Washington, died on July 23, 1885.
